flags.text: Check: The CTA says 'Try Kin free' but doesn't state the 14-day trial length as required whenever 'free' appears.
Check: 'free' appears in the CTA without stating the 14-day trial length there, even though it's stated elsewhere in the brief as required wherever 'free' appears.

Check: 'Kin reads your calendar' touches on data access sensitivities. Calendar isn't messages, but paired with 'reads' phrasing it may still raise wariness given local sensitivity around apps accessing personal data.
Check: Headline uses 'sorted', which matches ZA-V4 guidance well, but confirm the rest of the copy doesn't lean into any imported American phrasing elsewhere.

Check: 'Kin reads your inbox and your calendar' states the app accesses personal messages and schedule data. This risks reading as invasive given online fraud concerns unless purpose and control are made clearer.
Check: Personal data use (reading inbox/calendar) should have a clear lawful basis and stated purpose per NDPA; the ad doesn't clarify how this data is used or controlled.
Check: 'chases' is used here for chasing a refund. The snapshot flags this word as one that may read differently regionally, with no further guidance available.
Check: 'Kin reads your inbox and your calendar' states data access without clarifying purpose/control, which invites scrutiny under data-rights awareness norms.
Check: 'Try Kin free for 14 days' does state the length, but doesn't say what happens when the free period ends, which the mandatory requires alongside cost-of-living sensitivity.
Check: Dentist rebooking references NHS-adjacent life admin, which can read as flippant given how politically sensitive NHS/dentist waits are.
Check: The free trial rolling into a paid plan may need to meet DMCC Act 2024 subscription-contract disclosure rules, which aren't confirmed here.
